--- title: "Missing Values" subtitle: "≈ `NA` · `is.na()` · `replace_na()` · `fill()` · `complete()`" jupyter: python3 --- R has one missing marker, `NA`, and treats `NaN` as a kind of `NA`. Polars has two unrelated things: **null**, a missing value in any dtype, and **`NaN`**, an ordinary float value. Null tools ignore `NaN`, and aggregations skip nulls without being asked. This chapter covers how each one arises and propagates, how to count, fill and drop them, and how to find rows that are missing entirely. ## In tidyverse {#sec-na-tidyverse} ```r library(tidyverse) x <- c(1, NA, 0 / 0) # NA and NaN in one double vector is.na(x) # FALSE TRUE TRUE: NaN counts as missing mean(x) # NA: R makes you decide mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) # 1: na.rm drops NA *and* NaN df |> mutate(y = replace_na(y, 0), z = na_if(z, -999), w = coalesce(a, b)) df |> group_by(id) |> fill(dose, .direction = "down") stocks |> complete(year, qtr) # implicit → explicit flights |> distinct(tailnum) |> anti_join(planes) # find implicit gaps ``` R's rule: missingness is contagious. Arithmetic, comparisons and summaries all return `NA` until you opt out with `na.rm = TRUE`. Polars keeps contagion for element-wise operations but **not** for aggregations, and it never treats `NaN` as missing. ## Mental model {#sec-na-model} ```text A Float64 column holding [1.0, null, NaN] values │ 1.0 │ · │ NaN │ validity │ 1 │ 0 │ 1 │ null = validity bit 0; NaN = a valid float value null NaN dtypes every dtype Float16 / Float32 / Float64 only comes from None, empty CSV field, failed cast, 0/0, sqrt(-1), log(-1), shift(), outer joins, pivot gaps "NaN" in a CSV float column detect is_null() is_nan() (null → null) aggregations skipped propagate: mean, sum → NaN equality null == null → null NaN == NaN → true R analog NA NaN, but R's is.na(NaN) is TRUE ``` The validity bit is explained in [Data Model](../core/data-model.qmd#sec-dm-model). Each tool family sees only its own kind: | Task | null | `NaN` | |---|---|---| | detect | `is_null()`, `is_not_null()` | `is_nan()`, `is_not_nan()` | | count | `null_count()` | `is_nan().sum()` | | replace | `fill_null()` | `fill_nan()` | | drop rows | `drop_nulls()` | `drop_nans()` | | convert | — | `fill_nan(None)` turns `NaN` into null | : Two markers, two tool families {.striped} ## Mechanics {#sec-na-mechanics} ::: {#48ed8668 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} import datetime as dt import polars as pl import polars.selectors as cs from pl_notes import datasets penguins_df = datasets.penguins() flights_df = datasets.flights() weather_df = datasets.weather() planes_df = datasets.planes() airports_df = datasets.airports() ``` ::: ### Null vs NaN {#sec-na-nan} `NaN` comes from float arithmetic that has no answer. Null comes from missing input, and passes through arithmetic as null: ::: {#cf836068 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} ratio_df = pl.DataFrame({"num": [0.0, -1.0, 1.0, None], "den": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0]}) ratio_df.with_columns( ratio=pl.col("num") / pl.col("den"), sqrt=pl.col("num").sqrt(), ).with_columns( is_null=pl.col("ratio").is_null(), is_nan=pl.col("ratio").is_nan(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: `1 / 0` is `inf`, not `NaN`. `is_nan()` of a null is null, not `false`. Integer `//` and `%` by zero give null rather than an error. In a CSV, an empty field is null, and the string `NaN` in a float column parses as `NaN`. Unlike readr (default `na = c("", "NA")`), Polars does not read `NA` as missing unless you pass `null_values="NA"`, which is what `pl_notes.datasets` does: ::: {#e977264f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} pl.read_csv(b"reading,site\n1.5,A\nNaN,NA\n,B\n") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: **A realistic `NaN`.** Each hour's share of the day's rainfall is `precip / daily total`. On a dry day that is `0 / 0`: ::: {#89f72a1a .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df_share = weather_df.with_columns( precip_share=pl.col("precip") / pl.col("precip").sum().over("origin", "month", "day") ) weather_df_share.select( null_count=pl.col("precip_share").null_count(), nan_count=pl.col("precip_share").is_nan().sum(), mean=pl.col("precip_share").mean(), mean_rainy=pl.col("precip_share").fill_nan(None).mean(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Two thirds of the column is `NaN`, `null_count()` reports zero, and one `NaN` poisons the mean. `fill_nan(None)` converts `NaN` to null, after which `mean()` skips them. In R, `is.na()` and `na.rm = TRUE` would have handled both. **`NaN` is a value with a place in the order.** Polars treats `NaN` as equal to itself and greater than `inf`, so it sorts and groups predictably. `max()` skips it, though, while `mean()` propagates it: ::: {#6d5d1cc5 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = pl.Series("x", [3.0, float("nan"), float("inf"), None, 1.0]) { "x == x": (x == x).to_list(), "sort()": x.sort().to_list(), "max(), nan_max()": (x.max(), x.nan_max()), "mean()": x.mean(), "n_unique()": x.n_unique(), } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` {'x == x': [True, True, True, None, True], 'sort()': [None, 1.0, 3.0, inf, nan], 'max(), nan_max()': (inf, nan), 'mean()': nan, 'n_unique()': 5} ``` ::: ::: In R, `NaN == NaN` is `NA`, `sort()` drops `NaN`, and `max(c(1, NaN))` is `NaN`. ### How nulls propagate {#sec-na-propagation} Every row below was verified on Polars 2.0. `x` is a column with nulls. | Operation | Polars | R | |---|---|---| | `x + 1`, `x * 0`, `x ** 0` | null | `NA`, `NA`, but `NA^0` is `1` | | `x > 1`, `x == x` | null | `NA` | | `x.eq_missing(y)`, `x.ne_missing(y)` | null == null → `true`, never null | — | | `null & False`, `null | True` | `false`, `true` (Kleene logic) | same | | `null & True`, `null | False`, `~null` | null | same | | `x.sum()` | skips nulls; all-null → `0` | `sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)`; all-`NA` → `0` | | `x.mean()`, `median()`, `std()` | skip nulls; all-null → null | `mean(NA, na.rm = TRUE)` → `NaN` | | `x.min()`, `x.max()` | skip nulls; all-null → null | `max(NA, na.rm = TRUE)` → `-Inf` + warning | | `x.count()` / `x.len()` | non-null rows / all rows | `sum(!is.na(x))` / `n()` | | `x.n_unique()`, `unique()`, `group_by()` keys | null is one value, its own group | same | | `x.first()` | the first row, even if null; `ignore_nulls=True` skips | `first(x, na_rm = TRUE)` | | `x.cum_sum()` | null stays null, the sum carries on after it | `cumsum()` is `NA` from there on | | `x.any()`, `x.all()` | skip nulls (`ignore_nulls=True` default) | Kleene: `any(c(FALSE, NA))` → `NA`, `any(c(TRUE, NA))` → `TRUE` | | `pl.any_horizontal()`, `pl.all_horizontal()` | Kleene logic, like `|` and `&` | `x | y`, `x & y` | | `pl.sum_horizontal()` | skips nulls; all-null → `0` | `rowSums(na.rm = TRUE)` | | `x.is_in(["a", None])` | null → null; `nulls_equal=True` → `true` | `NA %in% c("a", NA)` → `TRUE` | | `x.str.*` | null → null | same | | `pl.concat_str()` | any null input → null; `ignore_nulls=True` | `str_c()` → `NA`; `paste()` → `"NA"` | | `when(cond)` with null `cond` | falls through to `otherwise()` | `case_when()`: to `.default`; `if_else()`: `NA` | | `filter(cond)` with null `cond` | row dropped | same | | `sort()` | nulls **first**, in both directions | `arrange()`: `NA` last | | `join()` keys | null never matches null; `nulls_equal=True` | `na_matches = "na"`: `NA` matches `NA` | : Null propagation, operation by operation {.striped} **Kleene logic** treats null as "true or false, unknown". `null & False` is `false` whatever the unknown is, so the answer is known. R does exactly the same, so this is one place where R intuition is right: ::: {#fe7813c3 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} bool_df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [True, False, None]}, schema={"a": pl.Boolean}) bool_df.join(bool_df.rename({"a": "b"}), how="cross").with_columns( a_and_b=pl.col("a") & pl.col("b"), a_or_b=pl.col("a") | pl.col("b"), not_a=~pl.col("a"), ).filter(pl.col("a").is_null()).sort("b", descending=True, nulls_last=True) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ```{=html}

Test `.is_null()` in the first branch if you need a separate label. **Joins** never match null keys, but they do match `NaN` keys, because `NaN` is a value (more in [Joins](../transform/joins.qmd)): ::: {#5678499f .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} left_df = pl.DataFrame({"key": [1.0, float("nan"), None], "left": ["a", "b", "c"]}) right_df = pl.DataFrame({"key": [1.0, float("nan"), None], "right": ["x", "y", "z"]}) left_df.join(right_df, on="key", how="inner") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

Per row, sum the `is_null()` flags horizontally (≈ `rowSums(is.na(df))`). Two penguins are missing every measurement and `sex`, and nine more are missing only `sex`: ::: {#43fab7c7 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins_df.with_columns(n_missing=pl.sum_horizontal(pl.all().is_null())).group_by( "n_missing" ).len().sort("n_missing") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

Missingness often has structure; the `flights` example is in @sec-na-mean-trap. ### Filling {#sec-na-filling} `fill_null()` takes a value, an expression, or a `strategy=`: ::: {#8439d4bf .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} dose = pl.Series("dose", [None, 1, None, None, 4, None]) pl.DataFrame(dose).with_columns( forward=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="forward"), # tidyr fill() "down" forward_1=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="forward", limit=1), backward=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="backward"), # "up" mean=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="mean"), zero=pl.col("dose").fill_null(strategy="zero"), linear=pl.col("dose").interpolate(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=13} ```{=html}

Leading and trailing nulls stay null when there is nothing to carry. Note that `mean` is `2`, not `2.5`: see @sec-na-fill-dtype. **Fill within groups** (≈ `group_by(patient) |> fill(dose_mg)`). Forward filling follows row order, so if rows are not in time order, pass `order_by=`: ::: {#b16a26db .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} visits_df = pl.DataFrame({ "patient": ["A", "B", "A", "B", "A", "B"], "day": [1, 1, 3, 2, 2, 3], "dose_mg": [10, None, None, 5, 20, None], }) visits_df.with_columns( by_row=pl.col("dose_mg").fill_null(strategy="forward").over("patient"), by_day=pl.col("dose_mg").fill_null(strategy="forward").over("patient", order_by="day"), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}

To drop rows, `drop_nulls()` checks every column and `subset=` limits it (≈ `drop_na(body_mass_g)`); `drop_nans()` is the `NaN` twin and keeps nulls: ::: {#6fe9fb6a .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} { "rows": penguins_df.height, "drop_nulls()": penguins_df.drop_nulls().height, "drop_nulls(subset='body_mass_g')": penguins_df.drop_nulls(subset="body_mass_g").height, "drop_nans() on precip_share": weather_df_share.drop_nans().height, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=18} ``` {'rows': 344, 'drop_nulls()': 333, "drop_nulls(subset='body_mass_g')": 342, 'drop_nans() on precip_share': 8474} ``` ::: ::: ### Explicit vs implicit missing {#sec-na-implicit} R4DS separates two kinds of missing data. An **explicit** missing value is a null in a row that exists. An **implicit** missing value is a row that should exist but doesn't. Every tool so far only sees explicit nulls. ```text stocks (7 rows) pivot(on="qtr") complete(year, qtr) year qtr price year 1 2 3 4 2020 4 null ← explicit 2020 4 null ← explicit 2020 1.88 0.59 0.35 null 2021 1 null ← was implicit (2021 Q1 has no row) 2021 null 0.92 0.17 2.66 ``` `complete()` is a cross join of the key values plus a left join back. A flag column added before the join records which rows were observed, so the two kinds stay distinguishable afterwards: ::: {#596cfee3 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} stocks_df = pl.DataFrame({ "year": [2020, 2020, 2020, 2020, 2021, 2021, 2021], "qtr": [1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 3, 4], "price": [1.88, 0.59, 0.35, None, 0.92, 0.17, 2.66], }) stocks_df_complete = ( stocks_df.select("year").unique() .join(stocks_df.select("qtr").unique(), how="cross") .join(stocks_df.with_columns(observed=pl.lit(True)), on=["year", "qtr"], how="left") .sort("year", "qtr") ) stocks_df_complete.filter(pl.col("price").is_null()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=19} ```{=html}

Pivoting is covered in [Reshaping](../transform/reshape.qmd). **Find the gaps with an anti-join.** `weather` should have one row per airport per hour of 2013. `complete()` only knows values that appear somewhere, so a full calendar has to come from outside the data (≈ `full_seq()`): ::: {#0b5a98d7 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} hours_df = pl.DataFrame({ "time_hour": pl.datetime_range( dt.datetime(2013, 1, 1), dt.datetime(2013, 12, 31, 23), interval="1h", time_zone="America/New_York", eager=True, ) }) weather_grid_df = weather_df.select("origin").unique().join(hours_df, how="cross") weather_df_gaps = weather_grid_df.join(weather_df, on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="anti") weather_df_gaps.group_by("origin").len().sort("origin") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=20} ```{=html}

To fill the gaps, make them explicit with a left join, then interpolate along time within each station: ::: {#c4654b58 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} weather_df_hourly = ( weather_grid_df.join(weather_df, on=["origin", "time_hour"], how="left") .sort("origin", "time_hour") .with_columns(temp_filled=pl.col("temp").interpolate_by("time_hour").over("origin")) ) weather_df_hourly.select( temp_nulls=pl.col("temp").null_count(), temp_filled_nulls=pl.col("temp_filled").null_count(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=21} ```{=html}

The 90 left after interpolating are those 30 edge hours per station, because interpolation needs a value on both sides. **Keys in one table, missing from another.** The R4DS examples translate directly. Four destinations are missing from `airports`, and 722 tail numbers (one of them null) are missing from `planes`: ::: {#f22423d9 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} { "dest not in airports": flights_df.select("dest").unique() .join(airports_df, left_on="dest", right_on="faa", how="anti") .sort("dest")["dest"].to_list(), "tailnum not in planes": flights_df.select("tailnum").unique() .join(planes_df, on="tailnum", how="anti").height, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` {'dest not in airports': ['BQN', 'PSE', 'SJU', 'STT'], 'tailnum not in planes': 722} ``` ::: ::: The null tail number shows up because a null key matches nothing. In this case dplyr gives the same count, since `planes` has no `NA` key to match. **Empty groups** are implicit missing rows too. `group_by()` on an `Enum` returns only the levels that occur (there is no `.drop = FALSE`); to keep the others, left-join the summary onto a frame of all levels, built from `dtype.categories` ([recipe](categorical.qmd#sec-cat-recipes)). ## Where it bites {#sec-na-gotchas} | R behaviour | Polars behaviour | |---|---| | `is.na(NaN)` is `TRUE`; `na.rm` drops `NaN` | `NaN` is not null; null tools ignore it (@sec-na-nan) | | `mean(x)` with an `NA` → `NA` | `mean()` skips nulls silently | | `filter(x)` and `filter(!x)` both drop `NA` rows | the same with `~`: null rows are in neither half | | `replace_na()` refuses the wrong type | `fill_null()` can change the dtype | | `any(c(FALSE, NA))` → `NA` | `.any()` → `false`, but `any_horizontal()` → null | : Traps at a glance (the rest are in the propagation table, @sec-na-propagation) {.striped} Kleene `&` and `|` and nulls forming their own group are also the same in both languages. ### `mean()` hides how many rows it used {#sec-na-mean-trap} R's `NA` result forces a decision. Polars just answers, so check `count()` against `len()` when the nulls carry meaning. In `flights`, a null `dep_time` means a cancelled flight: ::: {#fc0d9b67 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} flights_df.select( n=pl.len(), cancelled=pl.col("dep_time").is_null().sum(), n_used=pl.col("arr_delay").count(), mean_arr_delay=pl.col("arr_delay").mean(), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=23} ```{=html}

It silently drops the 8,255 cancellations and 1,175 more flights that departed but have no recorded arrival delay. ### A filter and its negation don't cover all rows {#sec-na-filter-trap} `filter()` drops rows where the condition is null, and `~null` is still null. The two penguins with no body mass are in neither half: ::: {#1a549e08 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} heavy = pl.col("body_mass_g") > 4000 { "heavy": penguins_df.filter(heavy).height, "~heavy": penguins_df.filter(~heavy).height, "total": penguins_df.height, } ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=24} ``` {'heavy': 172, '~heavy': 170, 'total': 344} ``` ::: ::: dplyr's `filter()` behaves the same. To keep them, write the complement explicitly: `~heavy | pl.col("body_mass_g").is_null()`. Similarly, `filter(pl.col("x").is_not_nan())` drops nulls as well as `NaN`, because `is_not_nan()` of a null is null; `drop_nans()` keeps them. ### `fill_null()` and dtypes {#sec-na-fill-dtype} `replace_na()` refuses a value of the wrong type. `fill_null()` on an expression finds a common dtype instead: ::: {#98df4c20 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} int_df = pl.DataFrame({"n": [1, 4, None], "s": ["a", "b", None]}) int_df.with_columns( mean_strategy=pl.col("n").fill_null(strategy="mean"), # Int64: 2.5 truncated to 2 mean_expr=pl.col("n").fill_null(pl.col("n").mean()), # Float64: 2.5 n_as_text=pl.col("n").fill_null("missing"), # Int64 becomes String ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=25} ```{=html}

With `b` all null: ::: {#3eb15ee1 .cell execution_count=26} ``` {.python .cell-code} flags_df = pl.DataFrame( {"a": [False, True], "b": [None, None]}, schema={"a": pl.Boolean, "b": pl.Boolean} ) flags_df.with_columns( b_any=pl.col("b").any(), # nulls skipped → false b_any_kleene=pl.col("b").any(ignore_nulls=False), # R's any(c(NA, NA)) → NA a_or_b=pl.any_horizontal("a", "b"), # false | null → null ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=26} ```{=html}
